name: Complete alternate-day fasting

lead: Complete alternate-day fasting means eating normally on one day and consuming no calories on the next, repeating the cycle. It is the strictest form of alternate-day fasting; the modified version allows up to about 25 percent of needs on fast days.

People use it to cut weekly calories and lose body fat, which reveals facial definition and a leaner physique. Reviews of intermittent fasting report weight losses of roughly 2.5 to 9.9 percent in most studies and similar benefits to ordinary calorie restriction.

paras: Practitioners alternate full fasting days, usually with water and calorie-free drinks, with unrestricted eating days. Some combine it with resistance training. Results over weeks to months depend on intake on feast days.

Short-term effects reported include hunger, irritability, dizziness, nausea, headaches and impaired thinking, usually fading within about a month. Health bodies advise against it for pregnant or breastfeeding people, children, older adults and people with or prone to eating disorders; reviews report a small possible loss of lean mass.

chain: Zero-calorie days lower weekly energy intake
Leaner face and more visible muscle definition
angle.text: Alternate-day fasting is used to run a calorie deficit without daily restriction. As body fat drops, facial leanness and physique definition increase.

lead: Complete alternate-day fasting (ADF) is a form of intermittent fasting in which a person eats no calories on fast days and eats freely on alternate days.[1] It is distinguished from modified ADF, which permits up to roughly 25 percent of usual energy needs on fast days.[1]

In looksmaxxing it is used as a fat-loss method: fewer weekly calories lowers body fat, which many people associate with sharper facial angles and a more defined physique. Reviews of intermittent fasting report most studies finding weight loss of about 2.5 to 9.9 percent.[1]
Research on intermittent fasting, including ADF, has compared it with continuous calorie restriction and examined body composition, cardiometabolic markers and adherence.[1][2]
infobox: Modified ADF, up to ~25% of needs

paras: Wikipedia's intermittent fasting article describes ADF as alternating 24-hour fast days with 24-hour feast days, and labels the zero-calorie version complete ADF, a form of total intermittent energy restriction.[1]

Reviews report weight loss in most intermittent-fasting studies, and limited evidence that it matches continuous calorie restriction for weight loss.[1] A 2021 umbrella review found moderate ADF for two to six months linked to lower weight, BMI and cardiometabolic risk factors in overweight or obese adults.[1][2]

On lean mass, a 2015 review found no effect from ADF while a 2019 review found a small decrease.[1] Dropout in intermittent-fasting trials ranged from 2 to 38 percent versus 0 to 50 percent for calorie restriction.[1]

A 2015 systematic review reported minor short-term effects such as hunger, irritability, dizziness, nausea, headaches and impaired thinking, which reportedly fade within a month.[1] The US National Institute on Aging does not recommend it for the general public, and New Zealand's Ministry of Health advises against it for people with insulin-dependent diabetes.[1] It is not recommended during pregnancy or breastfeeding, for children, older adults or those with eating disorders.[1]

A review of intermittent-fasting types found effects on weight and diabetic parameters in humans comparable with calorie restriction in several studies.[2] Trials specifically of complete (zero-calorie) ADF are a subset of this literature; a 2017 JAMA Internal Medicine randomized trial examined ADF in metabolically healthy obese adults.[1]
